kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.image.p.text: Specifies the image pull policy for this image volume source. Allowed values are Always, IfNotPresent, and Never, controlling when the image is pulled.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.image.r.text: The image reference to use for this volume, such as 'nginx:latest' or 'registry.example.com/app:v1'.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.iscsi.text: Represents an iSCSI volume, used to attach a block storage device accessible via iSCSI. It includes configuration such as target portal, IQN, LUN, and filesystem type.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.iscsi.c.text: Whether to enable CHAP authentication for iSCSI target discovery.
Enables CHAP authentication for the iSCSI session.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.iscsi.f.text: Filesystem type to be mounted on the ISCSI volume (e.g., 'ext4', 'xfs'). If unspecified, the default filesystem type is inferred to be 'ext4'.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.iscsi.i.text: Custom iSCSI initiator name. If not set, the system default initiator name is used.
The iSCSI Qualified Name (IQN) of the target. Must be a valid IQN, typically of the form iqn.yyyy-mm.reverse.domain:identifier.
The iSCSI interface to use. Defaults to 'default'.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.iscsi.l.text: The iSCSI target's logical unit number (LUN) that the volume will use. It is a required integer identifying the specific logical unit to connect to on the target.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.iscsi.p.text: List of additional iSCSI portals (IP addresses or hostnames) for multipath connectivity. The primary portal is specified by targetPortal.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.iscsi.r.text: ReadOnly here will force the ReadOnly setting in VolumeMounts. Defaults to false.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.iscsi.s.text: secretRef is a reference to a Secret object that contains CHAP authentication credentials for the iSCSI volume. The Secret must be in the same namespace as the pod.
Name of the Secret containing CHAP authentication credentials for the iSCSI volume. The Secret must exist in the same namespace as the Pod.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.iscsi.t.text: The iSCSI target portal. This is the IP address or hostname of the iSCSI target, optionally with a port number (ip:port) when using a non-default port.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.name.text: Name of the volume, used to reference it in container volumeMounts. Must be a DNS_LABEL and unique within the pod.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.nfs.text: NFS volume source for mounting a Network File System export. Specify the NFS server and path in this object to make the share available to the pod.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.nfs.pat.text: Path that is exported by the NFS server. Must be an absolute path.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.nfs.rea.text: Indicates whether the NFS volume is mounted read-only. Defaults to false.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.nfs.ser.text: The hostname or IP address of the NFS server that exports the volume.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.persist.text: Configures the volume to reference a PersistentVolumeClaim in the same namespace, using the claimName field to specify which claim to mount.
The name of the PersistentVolumeClaim resource in the same namespace that this volume should use.
Specifies whether the persistent volume claim is mounted as read-only. Defaults to false (read-write).

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.photon_.text: Defines a Photon Controller persistent disk volume source, allowing a pod to mount a Photon persistent disk by referencing its disk ID (pdID) and optional filesystem type (fsType).
Filesystem type to mount. Must be a filesystem type supported by the host operating system, e.g., 'ext4' or 'xfs'.
The unique identifier of the Photon persistent disk to mount as a volume. This corresponds to the `pdID` field in the Kubernetes PhotonPersistentDiskVolumeSource.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.portwor.text: Filesystem type to mount. Must be a filesystem type supported by the host operating system, e.g., 'ext4' or 'xfs'. If unspecified, defaults to 'ext4'.
Mounts the Portworx volume as read-only. When set to true, the volume is mounted with read-only permissions, preventing writes from the pod.
The ID of the Portworx volume to mount.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.project.text: Projected volume source that combines multiple existing volume sources into a single directory within the pod.
defaultMode is the mode bits used to set permissions on created files by default. Must be an octal value between 0000 and 0777 (or decimal 0-511); defaults to 0644.
Specifies the list of volume sources to project into the same directory. Each entry can be a secret, configMap, downwardAPI, or serviceAccountToken.

The `cluster_trust_bundle` block configures a projected volume source that injects a Kubernetes ClusterTrustBundle into the container's file system, selected by name, signer name, or label selector, and mounted at a specified path.
Label selector used to filter ClusterTrustBundle objects by their labels. When specified, only ClusterTrustBundles matching this selector are projected into the volume.

A list of label selector requirements used to filter ClusterTrustBundle resources by their labels. Each requirement specifies a key, an operator (e.g., In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist), and a list of values.
The label key that the match expression applies to. This is the Kubernetes label key used in the label selector requirement.
The operator used to evaluate the label selector match expression, such as In, NotIn, Exists, and DoesNotExist.
A list of string values that correspond to the label selector match expression. This field is required when the operator is 'In' or 'NotIn' and must be empty for operators 'Exists' or 'DoesNotExist'.

matchLabels is a map of {key,value} pairs. A single {key,value} in the matchLabels map is equivalent to an element of matchExpressions, whose key field is "key", the operator is "In", and the values array contains only "value". The requirements are ANDed.
Name of the ClusterTrustBundle resource to project into the volume.

Optional specifies whether the ClusterTrustBundle can be omitted from the pod. When set to true, the pod will still start even if the referenced ClusterTrustBundle does not exist; when false, the pod will be blocked if the ClusterTrustBundle is missing.
Relative path within the projected volume to mount the trust bundle. Must be a relative path, not absolute.
The name of the signer for the ClusterTrustBundle to be projected. For example, 'kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-bundle'.
The config_map field defines a ConfigMap source for a projected volume, allowing the contents of a Kubernetes ConfigMap to be exposed as files in the volume.
Optional list of key-to-path mappings that specifies which ConfigMap keys to project and their target paths. If omitted, all keys from the selected ConfigMap are projected.
The key in the ConfigMap's data to project into the volume. This is the name of the entry in the ConfigMap's data map that will be exposed as a file.
Optional mode bits used to set permissions on this file. Must be an octal value between 0000 and 0777 (decimal 0 and 511).
The relative path within the projected volume where the config map item's data is exposed. This path is relative to the volume's root directory.
Name of the referenced ConfigMap.
Specify whether the referenced ConfigMap and its keys must be defined. If true, the pod will start even if the ConfigMap or some of its keys are missing.
downwardAPI configures a projected volume source that exposes Pod and container metadata as files to the container.
List of downward API volume files. Each item defines a path and a field reference or resource field reference to populate.

field_ref selects a field of the pod (e.g., metadata.name, metadata.namespace, metadata.labels, spec.nodeName, status.podIP) to expose as a file in the projected volume. It uses the ObjectFieldSelector schema.
API version of the schema the field_path is written in terms of. Defaults to 'v1'.
The path to the Pod field to expose, using dot notation like 'metadata.name' or 'spec.nodeName'.
The file permission mode bits, expressed as an integer (e.g., 0644). If not set, the mode of the source item is used.
The relative path of the file within the projected volume where the downward API field value is exposed. The path must not contain '..' and must be a valid POSIX path.
Selects a resource field (e.g., CPU or memory limits/requests) of a container in the pod to be exposed via the downward API volume.
The name of the container for which the resource field is requested. If omitted, this defaults to the first container in the pod.
Divisor is a string representing a quantity (e.g., '1', '100m', '1Ki') by which the resource value is divided to produce the output value. If not specified, defaults to 1.
The resource name to select, such as `limits.cpu` or `requests.memory`, from the container's resource requirements.
The path relative to the volume mount where the certificate chain is exposed for the pod certificate projection.
The path within the projected volume where the private key for the pod certificate is mounted.
The type of private key used for the pod certificate. Valid values are 'rsa' and 'ec'. Defaults to 'rsa'.
The maximum validity period for the projected pod certificate, in seconds. This limits the lifetime of the issued certificate.
The name of the certificate signer to use when requesting the pod certificate. This specifies which signer will issue the certificate, and must correspond to a signer name registered in the cluster.
Projected volume source that populates the volume from a Secret. Specify the secret name and optionally items to select paths from the secret.

A list of key-to-path mappings. Each item specifies a key in the referenced Secret and the relative path within the projected volume where that key's value should be written. Unlisted keys are not projected.
The key in the secret's data map to include in the projected volume. This selects the specific entry from the Secret's data field to expose at the corresponding path.
The permission mode bits (in octal) for the file created from this secret item. If omitted, the volume's default mode is used.
The relative path in the volume where the value of the secret key is mounted. If omitted, the key name is used as the path.
Name of the Secret to project into the volume.
If true, the secret is optional, and the volume mount will succeed even if the secret does not exist.

The service account token configuration for this projected volume source. This selects a Kubernetes ServiceAccountTokenProjection, which injects the service account token into the volume at a specified path with optional audience and expiration settings.

Audience is the intended audience of the service account token. A recipient of the token must identify itself with an identifier specified in the audience, and otherwise should reject the token. If not specified, the audience defaults to the identifier of the API server.
The duration in seconds before the projected service account token expires.
Path (relative to the volume root) where the service account token file will be mounted. Must be a relative path and cannot contain '..' to escape the volume directory.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.quobyte.text: Represents a Quobyte volume source to be mounted into the pod. This configures the volume to use a Quobyte storage system.
Group to map volume access to. Defaults to 'default' if not specified.
If true, forces the Quobyte volume to be mounted with read-only permissions. Defaults to false.
Registry represents a single or multiple Quobyte Registry services specified as a string in the format host:port pair (multiple entries separated by commas).
The Quobyte tenant that owns the volume. This is an optional field.
The user to map volume access to for this Quobyte volume. If not specified, the default service account user is used.
The name of the Quobyte volume to mount.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.rbd.text: rbd configures a Rados Block Device (Ceph) volume. It allows the pod to mount a Ceph block device as a volume, specifying details like the Ceph monitors, image name, and filesystem type.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.rbd.fs_.text: Filesystem type to be used when mounting the RBD volume, such as 'ext4' or 'xfs'. If not specified, the default filesystem type is used.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.rbd.ima.text: The name of the RBD image to mount.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.rbd.key.text: Path to the keyring file used for authentication with the Ceph cluster. Defaults to /etc/ceph/keyring if not set.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.rbd.mon.text: A list of Ceph monitor addresses (hostnames or IPs) that the RBD volume will connect to.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.rbd.poo.text: The name of the RBD pool. If not specified, the default is 'rbd'.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.rbd.rea.text: Indicates whether the RBD volume is mounted as read-only on the pod.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.rbd.sec.text: secret_ref is an object reference to a Kubernetes Secret that contains the Ceph authentication key for accessing the RBD image. The Secret must be in the same namespace as the pod.
The name of the secret that contains the authentication key for the RBD volume.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.rbd.use.text: The RADOS user name for the RBD volume. Defaults to 'admin'.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.scale_i.text: Volume source that represents a ScaleIO storage volume to be mounted into the pod.
Filesystem type to mount for the ScaleIO volume. Must be a filesystem type supported by the host, e.g., 'ext4', 'xfs', or 'ntfs'.
The host address of the ScaleIO API Gateway. This is required for accessing the ScaleIO system to provision the volume.
The ScaleIO protection domain in which the storage pool resides. This determines the scope of storage resources used for the volume. If not specified, the default 'default' protection domain is used.
Specifies whether the ScaleIO volume is mounted as read-only. When set to true, the volume becomes read-only; defaults to false.
Reference to a Kubernetes Secret that contains the ScaleIO credentials required to access the storage system.
The name of the secret in the pod's namespace that contains the ScaleIO credentials.
Indicates whether SSL is enabled for communication with the ScaleIO storage backend.
Specifies the provisioning mode for the ScaleIO volume. Allowed values are 'ThinProvisioned' (default) and 'ThickProvisioned', controlling how storage is allocated.
Name of the Storage Pool in which the ScaleIO volume should be created.
The name of the ScaleIO system (the storage cluster) to attach the volume from.
The name of the ScaleIO volume to mount.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.secret.text: Configuration for a Kubernetes Secret volume source, allowing the Pod to mount a Secret as a volume.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.secret..text: The default file mode in octal for files exposed by the secret volume. Must be an integer between 0 and 0777 (e.g., 0644).
Maps specific keys from the secret to file paths in the volume. Each item can specify the key, the target path, and optional file mode permissions.
The key in the Secret's data map whose value is exposed as a file. This is used when a Secret volume is configured with specific items to include.
Mode is the permission bits (file mode) for the item file, specified as an octal number (e.g., 0644). It defines read/write/execute access for owner, group, and others.
The relative path inside the volume where the secret key's value is written as a file.
Specify whether the referenced Secret or its keys must be defined. If true, a missing Secret or missing keys will not cause the Pod to fail and the corresponding volume is ignored.
The name of the Secret to use as the volume source. This must correspond to a Secret in the same namespace as the Pod.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.storage.text: Represents a StorageOS volume source in a Kubernetes pod volume. When specified, this configures the pod to mount a volume from a StorageOS storage system.
Filesystem type to mount. Must be a filesystem type supported by the host operating system, such as "ext4", "xfs", or "ntfs". If not specified, the filesystem type is inferred from the volume.
When true, the StorageOS volume is mounted as read-only. Defaults to false.
A reference to a Secret object in the same namespace that contains the StorageOS API credentials.
Name of the secret that contains the credentials for the StorageOS volume.
The name of the StorageOS volume to mount.
The namespace within the StorageOS cluster where the volume is located. Defaults to the pod's namespace if not specified.

kubernetes_core_pod.spec.volumes.vsphere.text: Configuration for a vSphere (VMware) volume that can be attached to a pod. This is a volume source type used to mount storage from a vSphere Cloud Provider.
Filesystem type to mount for the vSphere volume, such as ext4, xfs, or ext3. Defaults to ext4 if not specified.
storage_policy_id is the identifier of the vSphere Storage Policy Based Management (SPBM) policy to apply to the volume. It determines storage characteristics such as performance and availability.
Name of the vSphere storage policy to use with this volume. If not specified, the default storage policy is applied.
The path of the vSphere volume, typically in the format '[datastore_name] path/to/volume'.

kubernetes_core_pod.status.conditions.la.text: The timestamp (RFC3339) of the last time this condition was probed.
Last time the condition transitioned from one status to another. This is typically represented as an RFC3339 timestamp string.

kubernetes_core_pod.status.conditions.me.text: Human-readable message indicating details about the condition's last transition.

kubernetes_core_pod.status.conditions.re.text: A machine-readable, CamelCase reason for the condition's last transition.

kubernetes_core_pod.status.conditions.st.text: The status of the condition, indicating whether the condition is currently True, False, or Unknown.

kubernetes_core_pod.status.conditions.ty.text: The type of pod condition, typically one of PodScheduled, Ready, Initialized, or ContainersReady.

kubernetes_core_pod.status.container_sta.text: The resources allocated to the container, such as CPU and memory, expressed as a map of resource names to the allocated quantities (in string form).
The name of the resource to which this status applies, such as cpu, memory, or a named device.
A list of health statuses for the resources allocated to the container, where each entry includes a resource ID and its health condition (e.g., Healthy, Unhealthy).
A human-readable message providing details about the status of the resource claim allocated to the container, such as an error or warning message.
The unique identifier of an allocated resource, such as a device ID or resource handle, as reported by the resource driver.
The unique identifier of the container, including the container runtime prefix (e.g., 'docker://', 'containerd://').
The container image reference (e.g., `nginx:latest`) used by this container, as reported in its status.
The image ID (digest) of the container image, as reported by the container runtime.
The last terminated state of the container, if any, including details like exit code, reason, and timestamps from the previous run.
Represents the running state of the container, containing details such as the start time. This field is populated when the container is in a running state, and is part of the last observed state.
The timestamp indicating when the container was last started in its current running state.
Represents the state of a container that has terminated, containing details such as exit code, reason, and timestamps.
The runtime-specific identifier of the terminated container, typically in the format <runtime>://<container-id> (e.g., docker://abc123).
The exit code returned by the container when it last terminated.
The time at which the container terminated or completed its execution. Represented as a string in RFC3339 format.

A human-readable message providing additional details about the container's termination, such as why it exited. This field is set by Kubernetes when the container terminates with a non-zero exit code or due to an error.
A brief, human-readable reason why the container terminated, such as 'OOMKilled' or 'Completed'.

The numeric signal number that caused the container to terminate, if it was terminated by a signal (e.g., 9 for SIGKILL, 15 for SIGTERM). This field is set only when a signal was the termination cause.
The timestamp (in RFC3339 UTC format) indicating when the terminated container started.
Represents the last observed waiting state of the container. This object provides details (reason and message) explaining why the container is waiting rather than running.
A human-readable message indicating details about why the container is in the waiting state, providing context for the container's last state.
A brief reason why the container is in the waiting state, such as 'ContainerCreating' or 'CrashLoopBackOff'.
The name of the container within the pod, matching the container name defined in the pod's spec.
Indicates whether the container is currently passing its readiness probe, meaning it is ready to accept traffic.
A list of resource claim references that the container requires. Each claim identifies a ResourceClaim object by name.
The name of the resource claim, which must correspond to a ResourceClaim object in the pod's namespace.

Limits specifies the maximum amount of compute resources allowed for the container. Keys are resource names such as 'cpu' or 'memory', and values are Kubernetes quantity strings (e.g., '500m', '1Gi').
A map of resource names (e.g., 'cpu', 'memory') to the quantity requested for the container. These specify the minimum amount of each resource that the container requires.
The number of times the container has restarted.
Indicates whether the container has started its main process. This is true once the container has been launched, even if it subsequently exited.

The current state of the container, represented as an object that contains one of waiting, running, or terminated sub-statuses, with details such as reason, message, or exit code specific to that state.
The running state of the container, containing details such as the time it was last started.
The timestamp (RFC3339 format) indicating when the container started running. Present when the container is in the Running state.
Represents the state of a container that has terminated, with details about the termination such as exit code, reason, and timestamps.
The unique identifier of the container that has terminated, as assigned by the container runtime (e.g., containerd or Docker).
The exit code of the container process when it terminated. Typically, zero indicates success and non-zero indicates an error.
The time at which the container terminated, in RFC 3339 format (e.g., 2023-01-01T00:00:00Z). This field is set only when the container is in the terminated state.
Message regarding the last termination of the container, providing details on why it terminated.
The reason the container's termination occurred, such as `OOMKilled`, `Completed`, or `Error`. This field provides a brief, machine-readable cause for the terminated state.
The signal number that caused the container to terminate, if the termination was due to a signal. For example, SIGTERM (15) or SIGKILL (9).
The timestamp indicating when the container started, in RFC3339 format. This is part of the terminated state, providing the start time for a container that has since terminated.
The waiting state of the container, containing a human-readable reason and message explaining why the container is not yet running.
The message detail from the waiting state, indicating why the container is waiting (e.g., pulling image, container creating).
The reason the container is in the waiting state, such as 'CrashLoopBackOff' or 'ImagePullBackOff'.
Linux-specific user information for the container, including UID, GID, and supplemental groups.
The numeric group ID (GID) of the Linux user under which the container runs.
A list of supplementary group IDs (GIDs) assigned to the container's Linux user, in addition to the primary group, for permission checks.
The numeric Unix user ID (UID) that the container's processes run with in the Linux namespace.
The path inside the container at which the volume is mounted.
The name of the volume mount, matching the name of a volume defined in the pod specification.
Indicates whether the volume is mounted as read-only. If true, the container can only read from the mount; if false, it can read and write.
recursiveReadOnly indicates whether recursive read-only mounts are enabled for this volume mount. Allowed values are 'Enabled', 'Disabled', or 'IfPossible'.
The reference of the image used for the volume image, such as a container image name and tag (e.g., 'nginx:latest').

kubernetes_core_pod.status.ephemeral_con.text: The set of resources (such as CPU and memory) allocated to the ephemeral container, represented as a map from resource name to the allocated quantity (a string in Kubernetes quantity format).
The name of the allocated resource, such as cpu or memory.
Health status of the resource. Valid values are 'Healthy' or 'Unhealthy'.
The unique identifier of the resource allocated to the ephemeral container, as reported in the allocated resources status (e.g., device ID or volume name).
The container ID of the ephemeral container, as reported by the container runtime.
The image the ephemeral container is running with, as reported in its container status.
Image ID of the ephemeral container's image, as reported by the container runtime.

The state of the previous instance of the ephemeral container before the most recent restart. This object holds the same sub-structure as the current state (waiting, running, or terminated) and is populated only after a restart occurs.
Represents the running state of the container. Populated when the container is currently running, and includes details such as the start time.
The timestamp indicating when the Kubernetes ephemeral container last entered the running state, in RFC3339 format (e.g., 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z).
The last observed terminated state of the container, containing details such as exit code, signal, reason, message, and the timestamps for when the container started and finished termination.
The container ID of the terminated ephemeral container, as reported by the container runtime.
The exit code returned by the container when it last terminated, as reported by the container runtime.
The time at which the container terminated, in RFC3339 format.
Human-readable message indicating details about why the container terminated. This is typically the container's termination message, if any.
A brief reason for the container's termination, as reported by the kubelet. Common values include 'OOMKilled', 'Completed', 'Error', etc.
The Unix signal number that caused the process to terminate, if it was killed by a signal. For example, 9 (SIGKILL) or 15 (SIGTERM). Not set if the container exited normally.
The timestamp at which the container was started, expressed as a string in RFC3339 format (e.g., 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z).
The waiting state of the ephemeral container. It includes a reason and message describing why the container is in a waiting state, such as a missing dependency or an image pull issue.
Message regarding why the container is not yet running.
The reason the container is waiting, such as 'CrashLoopBackOff' or 'ErrImagePull'.
The name of the ephemeral container that this status describes.
Ready indicates whether the ephemeral container is ready to serve requests.
List of resource claims that specify additional resources required by the ephemeral container. Each claim references a ResourceClaim defined in the Pod's spec by name.
The name of the ResourceClaim that this resource entry refers to. Must match the name of a ResourceClaim in the same namespace.
The name of a specific request within the referenced ResourceClaim, used to allocate a particular request when the claim provides multiple options.
Limits describes the maximum amount of compute resources allowed. Each key is a resource name (e.g., cpu, memory) and the value is a Kubernetes quantity string (e.g., '100m', '1Gi').
Map of resource request names to quantities (e.g., 'cpu', 'memory') that specify the minimum amount of compute resources required for the ephemeral container.
The number of times the ephemeral container has been restarted.
A boolean indicating whether the ephemeral container has started successfully. It becomes true after the container has been started and remains true even if the container subsequently exits.
State represents the current status of the ephemeral container, including details of its waiting, running, or terminated phase.
Represents the running state of the ephemeral container. Contains the timestamp (startedAt) when the container started running, populated when the container is in the running state.
The timestamp at which the ephemeral container started running, expressed in RFC 3339 format.
The terminated state of the ephemeral container, containing details about its termination including exit code, reason, and timestamps (started at and finished at).
The unique identifier of the terminated ephemeral container, as assigned by the container runtime.
The exit code returned by the container process when it terminated. A value of 0 indicates success, while non-zero values indicate an error or abnormal termination.
The timestamp (in RFC3339 format) indicating when the container terminated. This field is set when the container process exits.
A human-readable message providing additional details about why the container terminated, such as an error or exit reason.
Human-readable reason for the container's termination, such as OOMKilled or Error.
The numeric signal code (if any) that caused the ephemeral container's termination. This field is set when the container was terminated by a signal rather than exiting with an exit code.
The time at which the container was started, in RFC3339 format (e.g., '2023-01-01T00:00:00Z').
Represents the waiting state of the ephemeral container. This block provides the reason and message explaining why the container is not yet running (e.g., pulling image, waiting to start).
A human-readable message providing details about why the container is in the waiting state.
A short, machine-readable reason for why the container is in a waiting state, such as ErrImagePull or CrashLoopBackOff.
The effective user of the container process, if known. This object contains platform-specific user identity information, such as Linux (UID, GID) or Windows (username).
Object that specifies Linux-specific user attributes for the ephemeral container, such as UID and GID.
The group ID (GID) of the Linux user under which the ephemeral container's process runs.
Supplemental group IDs (GIDs) assigned to the container process in addition to its primary group. These are Linux group IDs.
The user ID (UID) of the Linux user that the container process runs as.
Volume mounts specifies how storage volumes are mounted into the ephemeral container's filesystem. Each entry defines a volume name and the mount path within the container.
Path within the ephemeral container at which the volume is mounted, e.g., '/var/log'.
The name of the volume mounted. This must match the name of a volume defined in the pod's spec.
Whether the volume is mounted read-only for the ephemeral container.
Indicates whether the volume mount is made recursively read-only. Allowed values are 'Enabled', 'Disabled', and 'IfPossible', controlling the recursive read-only behavior of the mount.
The container image reference (e.g., `nginx:latest` or a digest) for the image-backed volume mounted by the ephemeral container.

kubernetes_core_pod.status.extended_reso.text: The name of the container that this extended resource claim request mapping applies to.
The name of the resource claim request as defined in the pod's specification. It serves as the key in the mapping to associate the request with the actual resource claim.
The name of the specific resource that fulfills the extended resource claim.

kubernetes_core_pod.status.host_ips.ip.text: The IP address of the host node on which the pod is running.

kubernetes_core_pod.status.init_containe.text: The resources allocated to the init container, such as cpu and memory, specified as a map of resource names to quantities in Kubernetes resource quantity format.
The name of the resource (e.g., 'cpu', 'memory') whose allocated status is reported in this entry.
List of resources allocated to the init container, as reported in its allocated resources status.
Health status of the allocated resource, indicating whether it is Healthy, Unhealthy, or Unknown.
Identifies the specific resource instance allocated to the container, such as a device ID for device-level resources.
The container ID of the init container, in the format `<runtime>://<container_id>` (e.g., `docker://abc123`), as reported by the container runtime.
The container image that the init container is running.
The image ID of the container image used by the init container, as reported by the container runtime.
The last observed state of the init container before its current state. This typically reflects the previous run's terminated state, including details such as exit code, reason, and message.
Represents the details of the container's last running state, such as its start timestamp.
The time at which the init container's last running state started, in RFC3339 format.
Represents the terminated state of a container, providing details such as exit code, termination reason, and timestamps for when the container started and finished.
The container ID of the terminated container, in the format <runtime>://<container_id>.
The exit code returned by the container process when it terminated. A non-zero value typically indicates a failure.
The time at which the container terminated, in RFC3339 format (e.g., 2020-01-01T00:00:00Z).
A human-readable message providing details about the reason for the init container's termination.
A brief reason for the container's last termination, such as 'OOMKilled' or 'Completed', providing a human-readable explanation for why the container exited.
The Unix signal number that caused the container to terminate, if it was killed by a signal; otherwise 0 or unset.
The timestamp (RFC3339) at which the container was started.

Represents the waiting state of a container in Kubernetes, indicating that the container is not yet running and is waiting for a condition such as image pull or dependency readiness. This object contains details like a reason and a human-readable message.

Human-readable message indicating details about why the container is in the waiting state. This field provides additional context about the reason, such as an error message or conditions preventing the container from starting.
A machine-readable reason for the container being in the waiting state, such as 'CrashLoopBackOff', 'ErrImagePull', or 'ImagePullBackOff'.
The name of the init container to which this status belongs.
A boolean value indicating whether the init container is ready, meaning it has completed its initialization successfully.
A list of ResourceClaim references that are used by this container. Each claim names a resource defined in the pod's resourceClaims specification.
The name of the resource claim referenced by this init container's resource requirements.

Resource limits for the init container, specified as a map of resource name to quantity (e.g., cpu: '500m', memory: '128Mi'). These limits define the maximum amount of a resource the container may consume.

Requests describes the minimum amount of compute resources required for the init container. The keys are resource names (e.g., cpu, memory) and the values are Kubernetes quantity strings (e.g., "100m", "1Gi").
The number of times the init container has been restarted.
Indicates whether the init container has started at least once. In Kubernetes, this field is true when the container has successfully started.
State of the init container, describing its current condition as a nested object with fields for waiting, running, or terminated states, as defined by the Kubernetes API.
The running state of the init container, indicating that it is currently running. This block includes the timestamp for when the container started.
The timestamp (RFC 3339 format) at which the init container started running.
The terminated state of the container, present when the container has exited. It includes details such as exit code, signal, reason, message, start/finish times, and container ID.
The container ID of the terminated init container, as reported by the container runtime.
Exit code from the last termination of the init container.
Time at which the container last terminated, in RFC3339 format.
A human-readable message providing details about the last termination of the container, such as the reason for termination.

A brief reason for the container's termination. This field is populated when the container has terminated, and contains a short machine-readable string such as 'Completed' or 'Error' that indicates why the container stopped.

The signal number that terminated the init container, if it was killed by a Unix signal (e.g., 9 for SIGKILL). This field is part of the terminated state and is typically set when the container exits due to a signal.
The time at which the container was started, in RFC3339 format, as recorded in the terminated state of the init container.
Represents the container's waiting state, including a reason and message indicating why the container is not yet running.
A human-readable message indicating details about why the container is in the waiting state.
The reason why the init container is waiting, e.g., 'ContainerCreating' or 'CrashLoopBackOff'.
The Linux-specific user settings for the init container, including UID, GID, and supplemental groups, as part of the container status's user information.
The group ID (GID) of the Linux user for the init container, as reported in the container status.
A list of supplemental group IDs (GIDs) assigned to the container's user in its Linux context.
The numeric user ID (UID) of the user under which the container process is running.
The absolute path inside the init container where the volume is mounted. This path must be an absolute path and must not contain ':' or '..'.
Name of the volume to mount. Must match the name of a volume defined in the pod spec.
Whether the volume is mounted as read-only. Defaults to false (read-write).

recursiveReadOnly controls whether the volume mount is recursive read-only. Valid values are 'Enabled' (mount and all submounts are read-only), 'IfPossible' (best-effort recursive read-only with fallback), or 'Disabled' (only the mount itself is read-only).

kubernetes_core_pod.status.node_allocata.text: The amount of the resource allocated to this claim, expressed as a Kubernetes quantity string (e.g., '1', '500m', '2Gi').
A list of resources representing the overhead associated with a resource claim, specifying the additional resources required beyond the claimed resources.
Name of the ResourceClaim that this status describes.

kubernetes_core_pod.status.pod_ips.ip.text: The IP address assigned to the pod. Typically an IPv4 or IPv6 address, as configured in the cluster.

kubernetes_core_pod.status.resource_clai.text: Name of the resource claim as defined in the pod's spec.resourceClaims, identifying which claim this status belongs to.
The name of the ResourceClaim resource that was successfully bound to the pod. This is empty if the claim is not bound yet.

kubernetes_core_pod.status.volume_health.text: A list of health conditions for the volume, where each condition includes a type, status (e.g., True, False, Unknown), an optional message, and the last probe time.
Human-readable message providing details about the volume health condition, such as the reason it was reported.

Reason is a machine-readable description of the cause of the volume health condition, providing a stable identifier (e.g., FailedMount) for programmatic handling. It may be empty if no information is available.
The status of the volume health condition, typically one of 'True', 'False', or 'Unknown' as per Kubernetes condition conventions.
The timestamp at which the volume health status last changed. This is a string in RFC3339 format (e.g., '2023-01-01T00:00:00Z').
The name of the volume that this health status applies to. This matches the volume name defined in the pod's spec.

kubernetes_core_pod_template.metadata.ma.text: The API version of the resource that the managed field entry applies to, such as 'v1'.
The type of fields managed, such as 'FieldsV1', indicating the version and format of the fields specification.
FieldsV1 holds the first JSON version format as described in the JSON patch spec.
The name of the manager that owns this field, such as a controller or command-line tool (e.g., kubectl, kube-controller-manager).
The type of operation performed by the manager. Allowed values are 'Apply', 'Update', and 'Delete'.
The subresource to which this managed field belongs, such as an empty string for the main resource or 'status' for the status subresource.
The time at which the managed field entry was applied, in RFC3339 UTC format.

kubernetes_core_pod_template.metadata.ow.text: The API version of the referenced owner object (e.g., 'v1' or 'apps/v1').

If true, and the owner has the foregroundDeletion finalizer, the owner cannot be deleted until this reference is removed. Defaults to false. Setting this field requires delete permission on the owner.
Indicates whether this owner reference is the managing controller for the pod template.
Kind of the referenced owner resource (e.g., Pod, ReplicaSet, Deployment).
The name of the owner object referenced by this owner reference.
The UID of the owner object, used to uniquely identify the referenced owner in the Kubernetes API.

kubernetes_core_pod_template.template.me.text: The API version of the object schema that the manager used to manage this object. Part of a ManagedFieldsEntry, indicating which version of the Kubernetes API the manager was using when it applied or updated the managed fields.
Indicates the type of fields stored in this managedFields entry. In Kubernetes, this is always 'FieldsV1'.
The fieldsV1 field is a JSON representation of the fields that are managed by the current operation, stored in the Kubernetes fieldsV1 format.
The name of the manager (e.g., a controller or user) that owns this managed field entry in the Kubernetes object metadata.
The operation performed on the field by its manager, recorded in managed_fields. Typical values are 'Apply' and 'Update'.
The subresource this managed fields entry applies to. For example, 'status' or 'scale'.
The timestamp when the managed fields entry was last updated by the manager. This is part of the Kubernetes managedFields metadata, which tracks the fields managed by each controller or user.
The API version of the referenced owner resource, e.g., 'v1' or 'apps/v1'.
When true, prevents the dependent object from being deleted until the owner is removed, coordinating garbage collection of Kubernetes objects.
Indicates whether the referenced owner is the managing controller of the pod template. If true, this owner reference points to the controller that manages the resource.
The kind of the referenced Kubernetes object, such as 'Pod' or 'ReplicaSet'. This matches the 'kind' field of the owner's object metadata.
The name of the owner object. In Kubernetes OwnerReference, this field identifies the owning resource by its name, used together with apiVersion and kind to reference the owner.
The UID of the referenced object, uniquely identifying the owner resource in Kubernetes.

kubernetes_core_pod_template.template.sp.text: The node selector term that defines the preferred node selection criteria. It contains match_expressions and match_fields to specify node label and field requirements.

A list of node selector requirements that specify the node labels that must be met for the preference. Each requirement consists of a key, an operator (e.g., In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist), and a list of values.
The label key that the selector operates on (e.g., `kubernetes.io/hostname`).
Defines the operator for the match expression, such as In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist, Gt, or Lt. It specifies the relationship between the label key and the specified values.
Values is a list of string values for the match expression. It is required when the operator is In or NotIn, and must be empty when the operator is Exists or DoesNotExist.

match_fields is a list of node selector requirements that match nodes by their fields (e.g., metadata.name). Each requirement specifies a key, an operator (such as In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist), and optionally a list of values.
The node field key that this requirement matches on, such as metadata.name.
The operator used to compare the node field against the specified values. Valid values are 'In', 'NotIn', 'Exists', 'DoesNotExist', 'Gt', and 'Lt'.
An array of string values used in the node affinity match field requirement. Must be non-empty for operators 'In' and 'NotIn', and must be empty for operators 'Exists' and 'DoesNotExist'.
Weight associated with the node affinity preference, ranging from 1 to 100. The scheduler uses this weight to calculate the sum of weights of matching node selectors to prioritize nodes.

List of node selector requirements that specify label-based conditions for node selection. Each requirement includes a key, an operator (e.g., In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist), and optionally a set of values.
The node label key that the selector matches against. For example, 'disktype' or 'kubernetes.io/hostname'.

The operator represents the relationship between the key and a set of values. Allowed values: In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist, Gt, Lt. For In and NotIn, values must be provided; Exists and DoesNotExist check key presence; Gt and Lt compare integer values against the key's value.
A list of values that must match the node label value for the key, according to the operator. Must be empty when the operator is Exists or DoesNotExist.

A list of node selector requirements for node fields (e.g., metadata.name). Each requirement specifies a key, operator (In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist, Gt, Lt), and values, used to match nodes based on their label or field values.
The node label key that this match field applies to. For example, 'kubernetes.io/os' or 'kubernetes.io/arch'.
The operator to use for the match expression. Valid values are In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist, Gt, and Lt.

The list of values for the node selector requirement. The meaning depends on the operator: for In/NotIn, these are the values that the key must match (or not match); for Exists/DoesNotExist, this field must be empty.

This block represents a single pod affinity term, used to express a soft preference for scheduling pods relative to other pods. It defines the criteria for matching pods and the topology domain for co-location.
Label query over pods to select the group of pods for which the affinity term applies. It matches pods based on their labels.

A list of label selector requirements. Each requirement is an object with a key, an operator (e.g., In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist), and a list of values. The requirements are ANDed together to form the effective selector.

The label key that the match expression applies to, used to select pods based on label values. For example, in a match expression like `{ key: 'tier', operator: 'In', values: ['backend'] }`, this is the `'tier'` part.
Specifies the operator for the label selector match expression. Valid values are In, NotIn, Exists, and DoesNotExist.
A list of values that the label key must match when the operator is In or NotIn. For the Exists and DoesNotExist operators, this list must be empty.
A map of key-value pairs that must match the labels of the target pods to be selected. All specified labels must be present on a pod for it to match the selector.

A list of pod label keys. When present, the scheduler uses the values of these labels from the pod being scheduled to add `NotIn` requirements to the `labelSelector`, excluding pods that have the same values. This prevents the affinity/anti-affinity rule from matching pods that belong to the same group as the incoming pod, avoiding self-pod matching.
A label selector for namespaces. The pod affinity term applies to pods in namespaces matching this selector, in addition to those listed in `namespaces`. If empty, it applies to all namespaces.
A list of label selector requirements for selecting namespaces. Each requirement specifies a key, an operator (In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist), and optionally a set of values.
The label key that the operator applies to in the namespace selector's match expressions.
The operator for the label selector expression. Allowed values are In, NotIn, Exists, and DoesNotExist.
A list of string values. This list is used only for the 'In' and 'NotIn' operators; for other operators, the list must be empty.
A map of label keys and values that must match the labels of candidate namespaces. Only namespaces with all specified labels are selected for this namespace selector.
Specifies the namespaces whose pods the labelSelector should match. If empty, it defaults to the pod's own namespace.
The key of a node label that defines the failure domain used to match pods for the affinity term, such as 'kubernetes.io/hostname' or a zone label. It must match a label present on the nodes.
The weight associated with the pod affinity term, ranging from 1 to 100. Higher weights give the term more influence during scheduling.
A label selector used to identify the set of pods that the affinity requirement applies to. It follows the standard Kubernetes LabelSelector schema, including matchLabels and matchExpressions.

A list of label selector requirements. Each requirement consists of a key, an operator (In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist), and optionally a list of values. All requirements are combined with a logical AND.
The label key that the selector applies to. This is the key of a label that must be present on the pod for the affinity rule to match.
The operator for the label selector requirement. Valid values are In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist.

The values for the label key referenced in this match expression. Required for operators `In` and `NotIn`; must be empty for `Exists` and `DoesNotExist`. Each value corresponds to a label value that must (or must not) match the pod's labels.
A map of key-value pairs that must match the labels of the target pods for the pod affinity rule to apply. All specified labels must be present on the selected pod.

Specifies a list of label keys. If the pod being scheduled has any of these keys, then a node is excluded from consideration if any existing pod on that node has a matching value for that key. This helps define anti-affinity constraints where certain label keys must not align. It is an optional field corresponding to `mismatchLabelKeys` in the Kubernetes API.

A label selector to identify namespaces from which pods are considered for the affinity rule. If omitted, only the namespace of the pod where this affinity term is defined is used. This field is a standard Kubernetes label selector object.

A list of label selector requirements. Each requirement specifies a key, an operator (In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist), and optionally values. The namespaces matching all expressions are selected for the pod affinity rule.
The label key that the selector applies to. For the pod affinity rule to match, the namespace must have a label with this key (and an appropriate value depending on the operator).
Operator represents the key's relationship to a set of values. Valid operators are In, NotIn, Exists and DoesNotExist.

A list of string values used in a label selector requirement. For operators such as 'In' or 'NotIn', this specifies the set of values the label key must match (must be non-empty). For operators 'Exists' or 'DoesNotExist', this list must be empty.

A map of {key,value} pairs that define a label selector for namespaces. Each key-value pair is interpreted as a requirement that the namespace must have a label with that key and value (equivalent to a matchExpression with operator In). All requirements are ANDed together.
A list of namespaces to which the label selector applies for this pod affinity term. If empty, the selector is limited to the pod's own namespace.

The topology key that defines the domain (e.g., kubernetes.io/hostname) used to evaluate pod affinity/anti-affinity rules. Scheduler uses this key to determine which nodes are considered for placing the pod based on the labels of other pods.

Specifies a pod affinity term: a set of pods identified by label selectors and a topology domain (topology_key). In this preferred anti-affinity context, the scheduler attempts to avoid placing the pod in the same topology domain as pods matching the selector, but does not guarantee it.
Label selector used to identify the set of pods that the anti-affinity term applies to. It supports matchLabels and matchExpressions to select pods based on their labels.

A list of label selector requirements. Each requirement matches a key, an operator (such as In, NotIn, Exists, or DoesNotExist), and an optional list of values. All requirements are logically ANDed to form the complete selector.
The label key that this match expression applies to. This is the label key against which the operator and value list are evaluated.
The operator represents the relationship between the label key and the set of values. Allowed values are In, NotIn, Exists, and DoesNotExist.
A list of string values that the label selector requirement matches. This is used with operators such as In or NotIn; it must be empty for Exists and DoesNotExist operators.
A map of key-value pairs. The selector matches resources (e.g., pods) that have all specified labels with exact values, used to select pods for the affinity/anti-affinity rule.
Specifies a list of pod label keys to match when selecting pods. Only these label keys are considered when determining pod affinity/anti-affinity, and they are combined with the label selector.

mismatch_label_keys is a list of label keys that are excluded from the pod's label set before evaluating the affinity term. If any of these keys are present on the pod, they are removed from consideration when matching against the label selector.
A label selector for namespaces to consider for pod anti-affinity. If omitted, only namespaces of the pods in the cluster are considered. This selector matches against the labels of namespaces.

A list of label selector requirements. Each requirement specifies a key, an operator (e.g., In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist), and a list of values. The namespace selector matches namespaces whose labels satisfy all the requirements in this list.
The label key that the selector operates on. Must be a valid Kubernetes label key.
The operator to use for the label selector. Valid values are In, NotIn, Exists, and DoesNotExist.
The list of values for the label selector expression. For operators like In and NotIn, this list contains the allowed or excluded label values. For Exists and DoesNotExist, values must be empty.
A map of label keys and values used to select namespaces. The pod affinity term applies to namespaces matching all specified labels.
The namespaces to which the label selector applies. If omitted or empty, the selector applies to the pod's own namespace.
The key of the node label that defines the topology domain. Nodes with the same label value are considered part of the same domain for this affinity term.
The weight associated with the pod anti-affinity term. Must be an integer between 1 and 100. It determines the relative importance of this term when ranking nodes for preferred scheduling.
A label selector used to identify the pods that the anti-affinity rule applies to. This ensures the pod is scheduled away from pods matching these labels.

A list of label selector requirements that define the pods the anti-affinity rule applies to. Each requirement consists of a key, an operator (such as In, NotIn, Exists, or DoesNotExist), and an optional list of values.
The label key that the selector operates on.
The operator represents a key's relationship to a set of values. Valid operators are In, NotIn, Exists, and DoesNotExist.
The list of values that the label key must match for the operator. For operators 'In' and 'NotIn', this must be non-empty; for 'Exists' and 'DoesNotExist', this must be empty.
A map of label keys and values. The pod must have all of these labels to match this label selector, which defines the set of pods that the required anti-affinity rule applies to.

A list of label keys from the incoming pod that are used to match against the labels of existing pods when determining anti-affinity. The values for these keys in the pod being scheduled are extracted and combined with the label selector to select pods to avoid co-locating with.

A list of pod label keys to select which topology domains the pod should NOT be scheduled in. The pod's label value for each key is compared to the topology domain's label value; only domains with differing values are considered for this anti-affinity term.
A label selector that identifies which namespaces the pod anti-affinity term applies to. If omitted, it applies to the namespace of the pod being scheduled.

A list of label selector requirements. Each requirement specifies a key, operator, and values, and all requirements are combined with a logical AND. Used to select namespaces by their labels for pod anti-affinity.
The label key that the selector matches against. In namespace selectors, this is the key of a label on the namespace object that the match expression evaluates.
Defines the relationship between the key and the set of values in the match expression. Supported values are `In`, `NotIn`, `Exists`, and `DoesNotExist`.
A list of string values that the key must match according to the operator. Required for 'In' and 'NotIn' operators; must be empty for 'Exists' and 'DoesNotExist' operators.
A map of label keys and values that a namespace must have to be selected. The namespace selector matches namespaces whose labels include all specified key-value pairs.
A static list of namespaces that the anti-affinity term applies to. If neither this field nor namespaceSelector is specified, the term applies to the pod's own namespace.

The key that defines the topology domain on which pod anti-affinity is enforced. It specifies the node label key (e.g., `kubernetes.io/hostname`, `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`) used to group nodes into domains where the anti-affinity constraint applies. This field is required.
The arguments to the container's entrypoint command. These are passed as a list of strings, and if not set, the container's default entrypoint arguments are used.
The command to run in the container, equivalent to the Docker image's Entrypoint. This overrides the default command specified in the container image.
List of environment variables to set in the container. Each item defines a variable name and its value or value source.
Name of the environment variable. Must be a valid C identifier.
The value of the environment variable as a literal string. This should not be set if value_from is specified.
Specifies a source for the environment variable's value. It can reference a ConfigMap key, Secret key, a field of the pod, or a resource field. It is mutually exclusive with the 'value' field.
Selects a key from a ConfigMap in the pod's namespace; the value of that key is used as the environment variable's value.
The key within the referenced ConfigMap whose value is used for the environment variable.
The name of the ConfigMap to select a key from.
Specifies whether the referenced ConfigMap key must exist. If true, the container can start even if the key is not present; if false or omitted, the key must exist, otherwise the pod fails to start.
Selects a field of the pod to populate the environment variable value. Supports fields such as metadata.name, metadata.namespace, spec.nodeName, status.podIP, etc.
The API version of the referent (the object containing the field referenced by fieldPath).
The field path to select, such as 'metadata.name' or 'spec.nodeName'. Must be a valid Kubernetes pod field path.
Specify whether the referenced key must exist. When `true`, the container can start even if the key is not defined; when `false` (default), the key must be present.
resource_field_ref selects a resource field of the container (e.g., requests.cpu or limits.memory) and its value becomes the environment variable's value.
Optional name of the container to select the resource from. If empty, defaults to the container where this environment variable is defined.
The divisor to divide the resource value by. Defaults to 1.
The resource name to select, such as 'requests.cpu' or 'limits.memory'. This specifies which resource quantity of the container is exposed as the environment variable value.

Selects a key from a Kubernetes Secret to provide the value for the environment variable. The Secret must exist in the same namespace as the pod, and the referenced key must be present in that Secret.
The key within the referenced secret to select the value from.
The name of the Secret in the pod's namespace to select the key from.
Specifies whether the Secret or its key must be defined. If set to true, the container can start even if the secret or key does not exist, and the value is treated as an empty string.
List of sources to populate environment variables from. Each item defines a ConfigMap or Secret reference, allowing environment variables to be set from those sources.
Reference to a ConfigMap to populate environment variables from its data.
Name of the referenced ConfigMap. This must be the name of a ConfigMap in the pod's namespace.

Specifies whether the referenced ConfigMap must be defined. If true, the ConfigMap may be absent and the environment variables from it are omitted. If false or unset, the ConfigMap must exist or the pod creation will fail.
Optional prefix to prepend to the keys of the referenced ConfigMap or Secret when populating environment variables. Must be a valid C identifier.

Reference to a Secret. All key-value pairs from the Secret's data are exposed as environment variables. The Secret must exist in the same namespace as the pod unless the 'optional' field is set to true.
The name of the Secret to reference. This Secret must exist in the same namespace as the pod.
Specify whether the referenced Secret must be defined. If set to true, the Secret may be undefined and the envFrom entry is ignored if the Secret is not found.
The container image to run, specified as a string such as 'nginx:1.25' or a registry URL.
The image pull policy for the container. Valid values are Always, IfNotPresent, and Never, which determine when Kubernetes attempts to pull the image.
Lifecycle defines lifecycle hooks for the container, such as postStart and preStop, which are executed at specific points in the container's lifecycle.
post_start is a lifecycle hook that runs immediately after a container is started. It can include an exec command or an HTTP GET request to perform initialization or setup tasks.
Specifies the exec action to be performed when the postStart lifecycle hook is triggered. This action runs a command inside the container.
The command to execute in the container as the postStart lifecycle hook. Supplied as a list of strings, where the first element is the command and subsequent elements are arguments.

Specifies an HTTP GET request to perform as a post-start lifecycle hook. The handler is executed after the container is started, and its success determines whether the container is considered started.
Host name to connect to for the HTTP GET request. Defaults to the pod IP if not specified.
A list of custom HTTP headers to include in the HTTP GET request. Each header is an object with a name and value.
The name of the HTTP header to include in the request. For example, 'X-Custom-Header'.
The value of the HTTP header, as a string.
Path to access on the HTTP server for the lifecycle postStart HTTP GET request.
The port to access on the container for the HTTP GET request. Can be a numeric port number or the name of a container port (as an IntOrString value).
The protocol to use for the HTTP GET request in the lifecycle hook.
The URL scheme (protocol) used for the HTTP GET request. Valid values are 'HTTP' and 'HTTPS', with 'HTTP' as the default.
The sleep action defines a pause for the container during the post-start lifecycle hook. It contains a 'seconds' field that specifies the duration of the pause, after which the container continues.
The number of seconds the container will sleep after starting, as part of the sleep lifecycle hook. The container pauses for this duration before the postStart hook completes.
Specifies an action that attempts to open a TCP socket to a given port on the container, used as a lifecycle post-start hook.
The optional host name to connect to. If not specified, defaults to the pod IP.

The TCP port number or named port on the container that the postStart lifecycle handler should connect to. Numeric ports must be between 1 and 65535, or the name of a port defined in the container's ports.

Defines a lifecycle hook that executes an action immediately before the container is terminated. The action can be an exec command, an HTTP GET request, or a TCP socket check, as specified in the hook handler.
Exec specifies the command to run inside the container when the pre-stop hook is triggered. It defines the action taken before the container is terminated.

Command is the command line to execute inside the container. It is an array of strings, where the first element is the command and subsequent elements are arguments. The command is run directly, not via a shell.
Specifies an HTTP GET request to perform on the container as a lifecycle hook. It configures the endpoint, port, path, and headers for the GET request used by the pre-stop hook.
Host name to connect to for the HTTP GET request. Defaults to the pod IP. You probably want to set 'Host' in httpHeaders instead.
A list of HTTP headers to send with the GET request in this lifecycle hook. Each header is an object with a header name and value.
The header field name to send in the HTTP request.
The value of the HTTP header entry to include in the HTTP GET request for the pre-stop lifecycle hook.
The HTTP request path to access on the server, such as '/healthz'.
The TCP port to connect to for the HTTP GET request. It can be a numeric port or a named port from the container's ports.
The protocol (HTTP or HTTPS) to use for the HTTP GET request. Allowed values are 'HTTP' and 'HTTPS'.

Configures a sleep action for the pre-stop lifecycle hook, which pauses the container for a specified number of seconds before termination. This is an alternative to exec or HTTP-based hooks, using the 'seconds' field to define the delay duration.

The duration in seconds for the container to pause before it is terminated. This is used by the pre-stop lifecycle hook's sleep action, allowing the container to perform cleanup or wait before receiving the termination signal.
Represents a TCP socket action for the pre-stop lifecycle hook, specifying the port (and optionally host) on the container to connect to before termination.
The hostname or IP address to connect to for the TCP socket action. If not specified, defaults to the pod IP.
The TCP port to connect to on the container. Can be a numeric port (e.g., '8080') or a named port from the container's defined ports.
LivenessProbe defines a probe that checks whether the container is alive. If the probe fails, the kubelet kills the container and restarts it according to its restart policy.
Exec specifies the action to take in the container; the exec handler runs a command inside the container and uses its exit status (0 indicates success) to determine if the probe passes.

The command to run inside the container for this exec liveness probe. It is executed directly (not through a shell), with the container's root filesystem as working directory. A zero exit status indicates success; non-zero indicates failure.
The number of consecutive failures required for the liveness probe to be considered failed, after which the container will be restarted. Must be at least 1; defaults to 3 if not set.
Configures a gRPC health check for this probe, allowing the liveness probe to check container health via a gRPC request.
The port number of the gRPC server to connect to for the liveness probe. Must be between 1 and 65535.
The name of the service to place in the gRPC HealthCheckRequest. If not set, the default behavior is defined by the gRPC health checking protocol.

Performs an HTTP GET request to the container's IP address on the specified port and path. The container is considered healthy if the HTTP response status code is between 200 and 399, or if the configured success threshold is met.
The host name to connect to for the HTTP GET request. Defaults to the pod IP if not specified.
A list of custom HTTP headers to include in the probe's HTTP GET request. Each header object contains a 'name' and a 'value' field.
The name of the HTTP header to set in the request.
The value of the HTTP header that is sent with the HTTP GET request during the liveness probe. This is typically a string corresponding to the header name.
The HTTP path to request on the server when performing the liveness probe. For example, /healthz.
The port number or name of the port to access on the container for the HTTP GET request. In Kubernetes, this can be an integer port number or a named port (string) defined in the container's ports.
The protocol (HTTP or HTTPS) used for the HTTP GET request in the liveness probe.
The URI scheme to use for the HTTP GET request, such as HTTP or HTTPS.
Number of seconds after the container has started before liveness probes are initiated. Defaults to 0.
How often, in seconds, to perform the liveness probe. Defaults to 10 seconds; minimum value is 1.
Minimum consecutive successes for the probe to be considered successful after having failed. Defaults to 1; for liveness probes, this must always be 1.
Defines the TCP socket check for the liveness probe. It specifies the port (and optionally host) to test connectivity to.
The hostname or IP address to connect to for the TCP socket liveness probe. If not specified, it defaults to the pod's IP.
The TCP port to connect to for the liveness probe. It can be a numeric port (e.g., 8080) or a named port defined in the container.
Specifies the duration in seconds that the pod has to terminate gracefully before being forcibly killed. A value of 0 forces immediate termination.
Number of seconds after which the liveness probe times out. If unspecified, the default is 1 second.
Name of the container. Must be a DNS_LABEL and unique within the pod.
A list of ports to expose from the container. Each port object can specify container_port, name, protocol, host_ip, and host_port.
The port number on which the container listens, which must be between 1 and 65535.
The IP address on which to expose the host port. Leave empty to bind to all host interfaces (0.0.0.0).
The port on the host node to which the container port is mapped. If set, the container is accessible from outside the cluster via the host's IP address and this port.
Name of the container port. The name is optional but if specified must be unique among the ports in the container and can be referenced by services and other resources.
The protocol that the container port uses. Valid values are TCP, UDP, and SCTP. Defaults to TCP.

Defines a readiness probe that determines whether the container is ready to accept traffic. If the probe fails, the container's endpoint is removed from the associated Service. Configuration includes HTTP GET, command exec, TCP socket, and timing parameters such as initial_delay_seconds and period_seconds.

Exec specifies the action to take in the container as a command execution. This is used to define a command to run inside the container to check its readiness; if the command succeeds with exit code 0, the probe is considered successful.

The command to execute inside the container as part of the readiness probe. It is an array of strings; the first element is the command and the rest are arguments. The command is run directly, not via a shell.
The number of consecutive failures of the readiness probe required for the container to be marked as not ready. Must be a positive integer (minimum 1); defaults to 3.
Specifies an action involving a gRPC port, used to perform a gRPC health check as part of the readiness probe.
The port number on the container that the gRPC readiness probe will connect to for performing the health check. This should be the port on which the container's gRPC server is listening.
The name of the service to place in the gRPC health check request. If not specified, the default behavior is defined by the gRPC health checking protocol.
HTTP GET action to perform against a container path and port. Used by the readiness probe to determine if the container is ready based on the HTTP response status.
The hostname or IP address to connect to for the HTTP GET request. Defaults to the pod IP address if not specified.
Specifies a list of HTTP headers to include in the readiness probe request. Each item is an object with `name` and `value` fields defining a custom header.
The name of the HTTP header to include in the probe request, such as 'Authorization' or 'Content-Type'.
The value of the HTTP header that will be sent in the readiness probe's HTTP GET request. Specifies the value for the header named by the 'name' field.
The HTTP path to request on the container's server, e.g., /healthz. If not specified, defaults to /.
The port number or name of the container port to send the HTTP GET request to. Can be a numeric port or a named port defined in the container's ports.
The protocol (scheme) to use for the HTTP GET probe. Allowed values are 'HTTP' and 'HTTPS'; defaults to 'HTTP'.
The scheme to use for the HTTP GET request. Allowed values are 'HTTP' and 'HTTPS'. Defaults to 'HTTP'.
Number of seconds after the container has started before the readiness probe is initiated. Defaults to 0 if not specified.
How often (in seconds) to perform the readiness probe. Defaults to 10 seconds; the minimum value is 1.
The minimum consecutive successes required for the readiness probe to be considered successful after it has failed. Defaults to 1.

Defines a TCP socket probe configuration for the readiness probe. The probe attempts to open a TCP connection to the specified port on the container; the probe succeeds if the connection is established. This is an alternative to HTTP and exec probes.
Optional host name to connect to for the TCP probe; defaults to the pod IP.
The TCP port number or named port to connect to for the readiness probe.

The duration in seconds that a pod is allowed to gracefully terminate after receiving a termination signal before it is forcibly killed. This field is part of the pod specification, not the readiness probe configuration.
Number of seconds after which the readiness probe times out. Defaults to 1 second; the minimum allowed value is 1.

List of resource resize policies for the container. Each policy defines how a specific resource (e.g., CPU or memory) should be resized and whether the container must be restarted for the change to take effect.
Specifies the restart policy for the container when its resource limits are resized, as defined in the container's resize policy.

Specifies the compute resource requirements for the container, such as requests and limits for CPU and memory, which the scheduler uses to determine placement and the kubelet uses to enforce constraints.
List of ResourceClaim references that the container requires. Each claim specifies the name of a ResourceClaim object in the pod's namespace.
The name of the ResourceClaim that this container requires. This name must match a ResourceClaim in the same namespace.
Name of the ResourceClaim that this container requests.
A map of resource names (e.g., cpu, memory) to the maximum amount of that resource that the container is allowed to use. Values are Kubernetes quantity strings (e.g., '500m', '2Gi').
A map of minimum resource requests for the container, with resource names (e.g., 'cpu', 'memory') as keys and Kubernetes quantity strings as values (e.g., '100m', '1Gi').
Operator used to define the matching condition between a container's exit code and the specified values in the restart policy rule.
A list of numeric exit codes that define the condition for this restart policy rule.
Defines the security settings for the container, including user and group IDs, Linux capabilities, and other security options.
AllowPrivilegeEscalation controls whether a process can gain more privileges than its parent process. Set to false to prevent privilege escalation (e.g., from setuid binaries).

AppArmor profile configuration for the container. Defines the AppArmor profile to apply, with a type (e.g., Localhost, RuntimeDefault, Unconfined) and an optional localhostProfile name when type is Localhost.
When `type` is `Localhost`, this field specifies the name of the AppArmor profile loaded from the node's local filesystem.
Type of AppArmor profile to use. Valid values are 'Localhost', 'RuntimeDefault', and 'Unconfined'.
The capabilities field configures Linux capabilities for the container, allowing specific capabilities to be added (add) or dropped (drop) from the container's effective set.
List of Linux capabilities to add to the container's permitted capabilities. Each entry is a capability name such as 'NET_ADMIN' or 'SYS_TIME'.
The set of Linux capabilities to drop from the container's default capabilities. Can include 'ALL' to drop all capabilities.
Run the container in privileged mode. This grants the container all capabilities and access to host devices, essentially providing root-level access to the host.
Specifies the proc mount type for the container. Valid values are "Default" (default behavior) and "Unmasked" (allows access to all host processes). Optional.
If true, the container's root filesystem is mounted as read-only. This prevents the container from writing to its root filesystem.
The GID to run the entrypoint of the container process. If unspecified, the default group ID of the container image is used.
Indicates whether the container must run as a non-root user. If set to true, the kubelet will refuse to start the container if it would run as UID 0, enforcing a non-root execution.
The UID (user ID) that the container process runs under. If not specified, the container runs as the user defined in the image or by the runtime's default.
SeLinuxOptions specifies the SELinux context of the container. It is an object that can contain the labels 'level', 'role', 'type', and 'user' to define the SELinux configuration.
The SELinux level (MLS/MCS), typically a string such as 's0' or 's0:c123.c456'.
